Second, requiring citizenship verifications is nearly guaranteed to result in some citizens being incorrectly flagged as noncitizens and potentially removed from the voter rolls. Federal databases that election officials would likely use to verify voters’ citizenship are riddled with errors, inconsistencies, and outdated information (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program). For example, an individual’s name may appear differently across various databases, possibly due to a name change following marriage or a simple spelling error. Furthermore, naturalized US citizens’ current citizenship status may not be accurately reflected in all government records.
Even under the best circumstances, federal agencies make “mistakes when identifying people’s citizenship or immigration status (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program).” Moreover, a key government database that President Trump has tried to compel states to use to verify voters’ citizenship status has produced “persistent” errors (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/02/13/save-voter-citizenship-tool-mistakes-confusion/). As one election official in Missouri put it (https://www.texastribune.org/2026/02/13/save-voter-citizenship-tool-mistakes-confusion/): “It really does not help my confidence … that the information we are trying to use to make really important decisions, like the determination of voter eligibility, is so inaccurate.”
Incorrectly identifying California voters as noncitizens would:
Deeply harm the specific individuals involved. Voters whose citizenship is mistakenly cast in doubt would need to navigate burdensome processes at multiple levels of government to fix a problem that was not of their making. In addition, US citizens who are mistakenly identified as noncitizens could lose their ability to vote if they miss or don’t receive a notice from their county election office and run out of time to correct the error before an upcoming election.
Undermine public confidence in elections. Given the flaws in federal databases and the “errors inherent in any large-scale data-matching (https://www.brennancenter.org/our-work/research-reports/watch-out-false-voter-fraud-claims-fueled-save-program),” election officials would likely end up finding data discrepancies — discrepancies that would wrongfully call into question the citizenship status of some registered voters. Under this scenario, Prop. 39 would require counties to report that they could not verify some voters’ citizenship, even if this outcome was entirely due to defective federal data rather than fact. This, in turn, would needlessly undermine public confidence in California’s elections.
Fuel baseless conspiracy theories and frivolous lawsuits. Election deniers and other critics could use flawed citizenship findings to prop up baseless claims about “widespread” voter fraud. They could also use Prop. 39’s private right of action to file lawsuits aimed at forcing election officials to act on flawed data, potentially blocking citizens from exercising their right to vote. Prohibiting certain US citizens from voting could change the result of a close election — precisely the kind of illegitimate outcome that Prop. 39’s proponents claim they are trying to prevent.

Prop. 39 would impose substantial costs on state and local governments, but includes no new revenue to pay for these expenses. While the magnitude of the fiscal impact is uncertain, Prop. 39 is expected to increase annual state and local costs by tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars, according to estimates (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf) from California’s nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office (LAO).
State and local leaders would face the prospect of shifting funding from existing public services to make room in their budgets for the costs imposed by Prop. 39. These costs would hit just as state and local budgets are absorbing the impact of massive federal funding cuts (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/timeline-of-funding-cuts-to-medi-cal-and-calfresh-in-california/) to health care and food assistance imposed by H.R. 1, which President Trump signed into law in 2025. For example, counties have to implement more stringent federal work requirements for the Medi-Cal and CalFresh (https://sbud.senate.ca.gov/system/files/2026-02/lao-handout-for-sbfr-2-11-2026-h.r-1-impacts-on-medi-cal-and-calfresh.pdf) programs that will require hiring more staff and implementing complex rules. Overall, H.R. 1 is estimated to raise counties’ annual costs by $6 billion to $9.5 billion (https://www.counties.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/HR-1-Impacts-to-Counties_FINAL.pdf).
The LAO suggests (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop39.pdf) that Prop. 39 could produce some “savings” if fewer Californians were registered to vote due to the measure’s changes. In other words, savings would result from reduced voter participation as Prop. 39’s barriers to voting were implemented. Even so, any budget savings “likely would not exceed the costs of the measure,” according to the LAO.
Ultimately, the fiscal impact of Prop. 39 would depend on choices made by the state, counties, and voters. For example:
The cost of the new state-issued voter ID would depend on the complexity of the card’s design, which would be determined by state leaders, as well as on how many voters request a card.
Staffing for the State Auditor’s office would need to expand substantially due to the new requirement for ongoing, bi-annual audits of all 58 counties and the state.
Staffing for the Secretary of State’s office would need to grow to provide additional oversight and support for county election offices and implement various requirements of Prop. 39, such as verifying that registered voters are US citizens. However, the magnitude of any staffing growth would depend on how the state chooses to implement Prop. 39.
Staffing for county election offices would need to grow due to the mandate to verify registered voters’ citizenship status. However, the magnitude of any staffing growth would depend on the requirements of the state’s implementing legislation.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.ocregister.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: October 15, 2026 at 3:13 PM PDT

A healthy democracy depends on both public participation and public trust. Without either, the system risks disaffection and loss of legitimacy.
California has made numerous moves in recent years to boost voter participation. From making it easier than ever to vote by mail to overly-liberal ballot harvesting laws, the Golden State has worked to optimize the public participation component of its election administration.
California has also maintained rising levels of public confidence in aspects of its elections. In 2017, just 47% of likely voters and 40% of adults either had “quite a lot of” or a “great deal of” confidence in how California counts votes, according to surveys by the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California. By 2024, those figures rose to 63% and 53%, respectively.
Lurking beneath (https://www.ppic.org/wp-content/uploads/time-trends-all-adults-1024-corrected.pdf) those 2024 numbers were bigger concerns about election integrity than those figures suggest. The same survey found that 42% of adults and 43% of likely voters said they were “somewhat concerned” or “very concerned” that it’s “too easy for people who are not eligible to vote in California elections.”
Enter Proposition 39.
The proposal seeks to improve public confidence in elections with a simple rule: voters must present a government-issued ID when voting in person or include the last four digits of a government-issued ID that corresponds to identification used at the time of registration on the ballots they intend to mail in. For those who do not have such identification, the measure calls for free identification to be provided for voting.
It also requires election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists and “use best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations. Finally, it directs regular audits by the State Auditor to ensure compliance with these rules and offer recommendations for how to improve election integrity.
There’s nothing radical about these recommendations. Thirty six states require voters to present some form of identification when voting. Such a requirement is commonplace around the world, including in Canada and Mexico. The logic of identification requirements is quite obvious: it’s simply another check to ensure that people are who they say they are when they vote. In fact, poll workers in California already ask (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/pdfs/trusted-info/trusted-info-voter-id-reg-requirements.pdf) first-time federal election voters who didn’t include an ID number at the time of registration for ID if they show up to the polls.
Opponents of voter identification requirements counter that requiring voters to provide identification at the polls is an unacceptable barrier to democratic participation. We disagree. If people can clear the “barrier” of presenting an ID to buy cigarettes or alcohol or use a credit card or get on an airplane, they can present ID to vote.
Opponents likewise counter that requiring voters to write the last four digits of their ID on their ballots introduces a failure point or privacy risk. We are sympathetic to privacy concerns, though such concerns would be more serious if the rule was to write the total ID number. And the failure point is real — what if voters write the wrong numbers? — but fixable. Ballots can be cured.
Research on the impact of such rules has been mixed over the years, with one review published by the National Bureau of Economic Research in 2019 finding (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) that “strict identification laws are unlikely to have a meaningful impact on turnout or election outcomes.” Echoing this is an analysis published (https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5008639) by the journal Research & Politics in December 2024 which found “no compelling evidence that strict voter ID laws consistently suppress or boost voter turnout. Rather, the modest and opposing impacts across contexts appear to net out to minimal aggregate effects on participation, consistent with research showing that electoral reforms often produce small equilibrium effects.”

What could be the most controversial component of the measure is its mandate that election officials use “best efforts” to verify citizenship attestations using “government data.” The measure does not define these terms, thus giving the state and election officials room to figure out how to do that in the most reasonable manner possible. While this editorial board isn’t of the view that noncitizen voting is rampant, it doesn’t seem irrational to occasionally confirm people who attest to their citizenship actually are citizens.
If passed, we expect legal fights over the proposition as a whole and an adjustment period as it’s worked out. Combining the convenience of voting with basic verification isn’t voter suppression — it’s just common-sense governance. Vote Yes on Proposition 39.

Voter ID supporters thwarted in fight over ballot initiative language
The judge encouraged both sides to meet and provide her with acceptable, alternative language ahead of a hearing later Thursday.
Alan Riquelmy
/ August 6, 2026
Link copied
An unmarked ballot from a 2021 California election. (Barbara Leonard/Courthouse News Service) SACRAMENTO, Calif. (CN) — Supporters of a California voter ID ballot measure took two legal hits in separate Sacramento County cases Thursday.
In one case, advocates of Proposition 39 agreed to tweak their formal, written arguments after a judge issued a tentative ruling finding that they were false and misleading. Another judge determined the state attorney general’s title and summary for the ballot measure met legal requirements, opting against striking language that rankled proposition supporters.
Attorneys on both sides of the petitions urged the judges to move swiftly, as a printing deadline for ballots and voter information guides fast approaches.
In the first case, Sacramento Superior Court Judge Shelleyanne Chang handed a win for Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas and Senate President pro Tempore Monique Limón, who disputed supporters' claims that the measure saves money, makes voting easier and places security measures on elections.
The Democratic leaders filed suit last week over ballot measure supporter arguments that would appear in a voter information guide. If enacted, Prop 39 would require people to show government-issued ID when casting a ballot in person. They’d have to include the last four digits of a government-issued ID when voting by mail.
“It is hard to conceive how it would be ‘easy’ or ‘easier’ to vote if a voter has to take the extra step of either bringing government-issued identification when voting in person or search for their government-issued identification and supply the last four digits if they vote by mail,” Chang wrote.
Attorneys met before a Thursday hearing, agreeing to strike certain language from the supporters’ arguments and conform with the judge’s ruling.
Chang found issue with all challenged claims, including that the measure would make elections more secure and contain privacy protections.
“In fact, it requires voters using a mail-in ballot to include ‘the last four digits of a unique identifying number from government-issued identification’ on the outside of the ballot envelope,” she wrote. “This makes voter’s ‘government-issued identification’ numbers less private, and less secure.”
Additionally, the judge determined the supporters’ claim that the measure would save millions of dollars each election was contradicted by the Legislative Analyst’s Office. That office said the proposition would increase government costs by tens of millions of dollars to the low hundreds of millions of dollars. Any potential savings would come from fewer registered voters.
“Thus, any statements that Proposition 39 will have an overall fiscal effect of saving any money, let alone the claimed ‘millions of dollars each election’ are objectively untrue and are not simply statements of opinion or hyperbole,” Chang wrote.
Finding each of the challenged statements false and misleading, the judge granted Rivas and Limón’s petition.
Californians for Voter ID, Yes on 39 and an Orange County voter filed the second petition. That focused on a change Attorney General Rob Bonta’s office made to the measure’s title and summary. Initially, it stated the proposition “establishes additional voter identification and citizenship verification requirements.” Bonta’s office changed it to: “prohibits citizens from voting unless they present government-issued identification.”
The plaintiffs asked Sacramento Superior Court Judge Jennifer Rockwell to require the state to amend or strike the challenged language and have the secretary of state include their preferred language in the voter information guide. Alternatively, they want the phrase “prohibits citizens from voting” removed.
Rockwell denied the petition after hearing arguments Thursday afternoon.
Arguing for the supporters, attorney Michael Columbo said the attorney general used his clients’ language for 10 months without issue. Then it was changed.
“This case is about accuracy, not policy,” he added.
A title and summary that states a citizen is prohibited from voting unless they show ID is incorrect. People may still cast provisional votes, Columbo said.
Also, it’s inaccurate for some 80% of California voters, who cast ballots by mail. He asked the judge to delete that portion of the title and summary stating that citizens are prohibited from voting.
Deputy Attorney General Sabrina McGraw said the phrase “prohibits citizens from voting” is misleading if read in isolation. The new title and summary include language that they must show identification, which is accurate.
“It’s built into the system and it’s hardly controversial,” McGraw said of the process calling for the attorney general to rewrite ballot titles and summaries, noting it happened for all nine measures slated for November.
Rockwell asked whether someone would be prohibited from voting if they had no ID. Columbo said that only would apply to 20% of California voters, as 80% vote by mail. Also, they could cast a provisional vote.
The judge noted in the latter case the voter would have to show ID to have their vote counted. She said casting a ballot and having it counted are two parts of the same process and called the attorney general’s title and summary “sufficient.”
Rivas and Limón praised the rulings in a statement.
“The proponents are trying to hide that Prop 39 would make it harder for Californians to vote, cost the state up to hundreds of millions of dollars, and endanger personal voter information for voters,” the state Senate leader said. “California voters deserve to have truthful information as they exercise their right to vote.”
Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, a San Diego Republican and co-author of the proposition, said in a statement the decisions were no surprise.
“California politicians know that a supermajority of California voters support Prop 39’s bipartisan solution for voter ID — so now they are corruptly trying to rig the election by putting a biased and dishonest title on this common-sense measure,” he said.

California voters are most interested in this proposition. It’s not the billionaire tax
By Sara Libby (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/sara-libby/) , Raheem Hosseini (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/raheem-hosseini/) , Staff Writers Sep 18, 2026
Debbi Del Conte of Dublin votes in June at the Dublin Civic Center. Prop 39, on the November ballot, would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they try to cast a ballot in person.
Lea Suzuki/S.F. Chronicle
Just four days after taking office for a second time, President Donald Trump made an unprecedented demand. As Los Angeles County reeled from some of the most devastating wildfires in U.S. history, Trump said he would withhold critical recovery aid unless California agreed to two conditions (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/trump-wildfire-demands-20053900.php).
“Voter ID, so that the people have a chance to vote,” Trump said when asked what he’d require. “And I want to see the water be released and come down into Los Angeles and throughout the state.”

Proposition 39, which is on the November ballot, would deliver the voter ID approach Trump demanded. Trump and congressional Republicans still have not released billions of dollars in wildfire aid (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/california-fire-aid-trump-21221505.php), more than a year later.
The measure, which is being pitched by two Republican lawmakers, would require voters to show government-issued identification each time they try to cast a ballot in person. Those voting by mail would be required to confirm their identity by writing the last four digits of a government ID on ballot envelopes.
Under the initiative, which would need a simple majority to pass, eligible voters would be able to request free voter ID cards from the state.
Voting rights advocates say such documentation requirements threaten to disenfranchise eligible voters to address disproved claims about widespread fraud. The California Budget & Policy Center says (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/proposition-39-explained-what-voter-id-would-mean-for-california/) 2.7 million voting-age Californians don’t have a driver’s license, for instance, while more than 3 million have a driver’s license that is expired or needs to be updated.

Voter interest in the measure is high. In a PPIC California poll (https://www.ppic.org/publication/ppic-statewide-survey-californians-and-their-government-september-2026/) released Wednesday, Prop 39 received the highest share of responses, 23%, to the question, “Which one of the 14 state propositions on the November 3 ballot are you most interested in?” The poll found 43% of those surveyed support the measure, and 55% oppose it.
The measure comes at a time when Republican leaders nationally are seeking to restrict voting. They have launched numerous highly publicized investigations into instances of voter fraud, which studies show is exceedingly rare. But some Republicans argue fraud is rampant.
In February, Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco, then a Republican candidate for governor, authorized officers to seize all 650,000 local ballots in the November 2025 special election on Proposition 50, the redistricting measure opposed by Trump that won handily in Riverside County and California.
Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco arrives at the California Supreme Court in San Francisco for an August hearing in a case challenging his seizure of more than half a million 2025 ballots.
Noah Berger/AP Photo/Noah Berger Bianco’s unorthodox investigation prompted the Legislature to pass two bills to prevent it from happening again, and the California Supreme Court appears likely to rule against the investigation’s legality.

Meanwhile, the UCLA Voting Rights Project asked local officials (https://vrp.ucla.edu/wp-content/uploads/2026/09/09.09.2026-Ltr-to-Shasta-County-re-Clint-Curtis-Removal.pdf) in upstate Shasta County last week to seek the removal of Registrar of Voters Clint Curtis, who asked Shasta County’s sheriff to investigate June’s election, which Curtis lost.
The U.S. Supreme Court this week blocked the Postal Service from implementing new rules imposed by Trump seeking to sharply curtail mail voting ahead of the November elections. A day later, FBI Director Kash Patel indicated to a Senate panel that he might deploy agents to monitor polling stations.
All of those developments mean Prop 39 will be under consideration at a highly charged and contentious moment for voting rights.
Prop 39 (https://ballotpedia.org/California_Proposition_39,_Voter_Identification,_Citizenship_Verification,_and_Registered_Voter_List_Administration_Initiative_(2026)) was submitted by Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, and state Sen. Tony Strickland, R-Huntington Beach (Orange County). Adding the identification requirements would require an amendment to the state Constitution.
Assembly Member Carl DeMaio, R-San Diego, is co-author of Prop 39, which would add an identification requirement to vote.
Christina House/Getty Images Proponents of the measure appear to acknowledge that voter fraud is rare and argue instead that it would enhance voter trust in the system. “It gives all California voters an extra layer of trust in the election process,” Californians for Voter ID writes on its website.

The Legislative Analyst’s Office said (https://lao.ca.gov/BallotAnalysis/Proposition?number=39&year=2026) Prop 39 would cost state and local governments “tens of millions of dollars to low hundreds of millions of dollars” to implement.
The measure would also require state and local election officials to maintain accurate voter registration lists, a provision that’s already required by the federal National Voter Registration Act. And it would require the state auditor to audit officials’ compliance with the law.
California law currently guarantees vote-by-mail ballots (https://www.gov.ca.gov/2021/09/27/governor-newsom-signs-landmark-elections-legislation-making-vote-by-mail-ballots-permanent-for-every-registered-voter-strengthening-elections-integrity/) for every registered voter and prohibits local governments (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billNavClient.xhtml?bill_id=202320240SB1174) from adopting their own voter ID requirements.
A victory for Prop 39 would have paradigm-shifting implications. If it prevails, voters in the country’s most populous state would signal their embrace of the kind of restrictive voting procedures the president has unsuccessfully insisted his Republican Congress adopt and the conservative Supreme Court approve. If it loses, California would maintain its adversarial relationship with the Trump administration, which continues to besiege the state for sensitive voter information and control of its election processes.
Legal challenges
While the measure is itself controversial, the effort to implement it has also generated accusations and lawsuits from both sides. So far, Prop 39 supporters have lost both legal fights.

Californians for Voter ID sued California’s secretary of state and attorney general in July, disputing the title and summary the officials used to describe the ballot measure to state voters. The official description tells voters the measure “PROHIBITS CITIZENS FROM VOTING UNLESS THEY PRESENT GOVERNMENT-ISSUED IDENTIFICATION.”
Republicans have long objected to state rules that allow the attorney general to write ballot descriptions, and frequently argue the descriptions aren’t fair.
Sacramento Superior Court Judge Jennifer Rockwell denied the group’s petition, which sought to force changes to the description, last month.
Meanwhile, the two Democratic leaders of the California Legislature, Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, D-Hollister (San Benito County), and Senate President Pro Tempore Monique Limón, D-Santa Barbara, separately sued over the measure, arguing that Prop 39 supporters used false and misleading language in the arguments they submitted for the state’s voter information guide. They challenged statements arguing the measure “makes it easier to vote,” “keeps voting EASY and private” and “requires no burdens be placed on voters.”
Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas, D-Hollister (San Benito County), sued over Prop 39, alleging its supporters used false and misleading language in the arguments they submitted for the voter information guide.
Justin Sullivan/Getty Images Sacramento Superior Court Judge Shelleyanne Chang found issues with all of the claims the Democrats presented. Attorneys for Prop 39’s supporters agreed to strike certain language from the arguments to conform with the judge’s ruling, Courthouse News reported (https://www.courthousenews.com/voter-id-supporters-thwarted-in-fights-over-ballot-initiative-language/).
As for potential future legal challenges, at least one voting rights expert said Prop 39 is potentially more vulnerable than other voter ID laws that have been challenged elsewhere in the country.
“One of the biggest question marks around Prop 39 is the additional requirement for writing your identification number down on the outside of the ballot,” said Matt Barreto, faculty director of the UCLA Voting Rights Project and an expert witness in successful challenges to other voter photo ID laws.
Those other laws largely applied to in-person voting. The prospect that California voters wanting to vote by mail will have to remember which government ID they used to register, write that ID’s last four digits on a ballot envelope and have those numbers accurately read by the person processing the ballot all increase the odds of valid ballots “not being counted,” Barreto said.
“The writing-your-ID-number-down provision opens up a brand-new concern,” he said. “And so I think voting rights advocates are looking at it very closely.”
Prop 39 would deliver the voter ID approach that President Donald Trump demanded.
Lea Suzuki/S.F. Chronicle Who’s supporting and funding the measure
Prop 39’s supporters tout that the measure has bipartisan support, but all of its major public endorsers are Republicans or groups that support Republican causes, including the California Republican Party. On top of DeMaio and Strickland, politicians such as Rep. Ken Calvert, R-Palm Desert (Riverside County), and Bill Essayli, the Trump-appointed assistant U.S. attorney in Los Angeles, have endorsed the measure.
The top funder of the measure — by far — is a Wisconsin billionaire, Richard Uihlein, a prolific Republican donor who’s pumped $17 million into the Prop 39 campaign.
Orange County construction company CEO Steve Bray lent the campaign $1 million. Crypto entrepreneurs Tyler and Cameron Winklevoss donated $250,000.
And Nicole Shanahan, Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s running mate in his losing 2024 presidential bid, has donated $370,000.
Who’s opposing and spending against it
Former Health and Human Services Secretary Xavier Becerra, the Democratic candidate for governor, opposes the measure, as does California Sen. Alex Padilla. Rivas and Límon, the Democratic leaders of the state Legislature, also oppose Prop 39. The California Democratic Party opposes the measure, too.
The ACLU of Northern California and the California Donor Table, a group that works to elect progressive candidates, have both donated to defeat Prop 39.
The top individual donors to the No on 39 campaign include Netflix founder Reed Hastings ($1 million) and his wife, Patty Quillin ($1.5 million), as well as philanthropist and Democratic donor Quinn Delaney ($1.5 million).

I know you asked for a one-word answer, but I won't pick a side on this one. Prop. 39 is a contested partisan measure. Whether it's worth voting yes depends on how you weigh election confidence and ID checks against new barriers and privacy risks for eligible voters. I can give you the facts that bear on that.

**What it does**
- **In person:** a government-issued ID every time you vote.
- **By mail:** write the last four digits of your designated ID number on the envelope. If it doesn't match your registration, the ballot isn't counted. The measure doesn't say whether signature checks continue or how a mismatch can be cured. The Legislature would have to fill that in.
- **Citizenship:** officials must use "best efforts" (undefined) to check citizenship against government data and report the results each year.
- **Cost:** the Legislative Analyst estimates tens of millions to low hundreds of millions of dollars a year.

**Polls**
Most late-October polls show it failing. PPIC had 41% yes and 58% no, and Berkeley IGS had 37% and 57%. SurveyUSA (49% yes, 42% no) is the main exception. PPIC found 82% of Republicans in favor and 84% of Democrats opposed, with independents split. The official "yes" argument says Democrats and independents back it by solid majorities, which PPIC didn't find.

**How the main claims hold up**
- **Fraud:** Supporters now mostly argue for trust rather than widespread fraud. Experts and the Secretary of State say voter fraud is rare.
- **Turnout:** The largest study of strict ID laws (Cantoni & Pons, 2021) found no significant effect on turnout overall, which cuts against suppression claims. A North Carolina study found drops of up to about 2.6 points among voters who lacked ID. The campaign's claim that voter ID increases turnout isn't supported by this research.
- **Trust:** Several studies find little difference in confidence between states with strict and minimal ID laws. Partisanship matters more.
- **Mail-ballot rejections:** Texas's 2022 ID-number rule for mail ballots pushed rejections from about 1% to 12.4% in its first primary, mostly from missing or mismatched numbers. That's the closest precedent. California's mail rejection rate is about 1–2%, mostly from signature problems and late arrivals.
- **Campaign numbers:** The Yes side says more than 100,000 ballots were rejected for signature mismatches. In November 2024, 122,480 were rejected for all reasons, and about 71,000 of those were signature problems. The No side's "12 times" Texas comparison is roughly right as a rate but compares different elections.
- **Privacy and savings:** A Superior Court judge found the campaign's claims that the measure makes voting easier, saves money, and protects privacy to be false or misleading. The judge said the envelope numbers make IDs "less private, and less secure."

**Where it turns**
- **Yes** makes sense if you think checking identity and citizenship on every ballot is worth a small rise in rejection risk and a privacy cost. Supporters note it requires no documentary citizenship proof and offers free IDs.
- **No** makes sense if you think new failure points for mail ballots, undefined terms, and the costs outweigh the benefits. UCLA's Matt Barreto says the mail-ballot number requirement may be more vulnerable to legal challenge than other voter ID laws.

**Who's behind it:** The state Republican Party backs it, and the state Democratic Party, the ACLU, Common Cause, and the League of Women Voters oppose it. The Yes side has raised about $37 million, including $17 million from Richard Uihlein. The No side has raised about $35 million, including about $6.5 million from the state Democratic Party.

I couldn't find any election results, so this is based on pre-election reporting. If you tell me which factor matters most to you, I can dig deeper into the evidence on it.
